real_qa.q: What is the main problem with how businesses are currently implementing generative AI?
real_qa.r: There is rushing and lack of forethought into what organizations will do with AI. AI projects look done when they are nowhere near done, and there is insufficient thought about keeping AI running well, productive, and at high degrees of availability and quality. People have skipped steps around governance, management, inspection, and applying judgment to AI solutions.
real_qa.requete: why businesses failing generative AI implementation

real_qa.q: How does generative AI transformation differ from previous technology revolutions like cloud computing?
real_qa.r: Generative AI is a bottom-up change where building with generative AI is the core activity, unlike cloud migration which could be top-down managed. With generative AI, non-deterministic behavior means leadership cannot create a prescribed plan; instead it requires iterative experimentation. All personas—engineers, non-technical employees, leaders, and customers—must actively participate in creation rather than reverting to traditional spec-and-deliver models.
real_qa.requete: generative AI transformation vs cloud computing

real_qa.q: What is generative AI and how does it differ from traditional software?
real_qa.r: Generative AI is any application using a large language model that orchestrates decisions and reasoning processes, or generates outputs like design, text, or email based on massive datasets. The key difference from traditional software is that large language models are non-deterministic—they do not always produce the same outputs given the same inputs—making workflows fundamentally different.
real_qa.requete: what is generative AI definition large language model

real_qa.q: How should businesses structure AI systems if they want to maintain control and not rely entirely on foundation models?
real_qa.r: Organizations will likely use a mixture of foundation models like Claude and Gemini for high-level reasoning components, but also create small language models tuned in-house, RAG systems, and tool calls that they maintain control of themselves. This creates multiple AI systems that need to collaborate agentic ally, which introduces complex observability and management challenges that currently have no dedicated tools, making it a critical gap Prove AI is addressing.
real_qa.requete: how to build AI systems with multiple models

real_qa.q: Who bears legal responsibility for generative AI systems that businesses build and deploy?
real_qa.r: Software professionals who build generative AI systems bear the liability, just as with any other software they create. There is no free pass for AI projects. Even if engineers do not fully understand exactly how an AI system is built, they are responsible for it, similar to how engineers have managed non-deterministic physical processes and engineered solutions for centuries.
real_qa.requete: AI liability responsibility who responsible generative AI

guest.bio_context: Greg Whalen began his career as an AI researcher in the late 1990s, working on predictive analytics in healthcare such as predicting length of stay post-cardiac bypass surgery. He has built SaaS software in digital marketing with machine learning components, ran a practice at Pivotal around 2013-2014 helping organizations implement big data analytics and data science teams, and worked for AWS before founding Prove AI to address governance and management challenges in generative AI systems.
